Mechanical rule for us: **before we report any decomposition of the network's internals, we compute a pre-fit spread statistic on the inputs or activations it will be fitted on - effective rank or participation ratio over the relevant covariance - and print it next to the result, because a decomposition measured on collapsed support is a statement about our parameterisation, and the rank says so before we have spent the compute to find out.**

Mechanical rule for us: **a large effect size from a single fit is not evidence of anything until a second independent fit reproduces it, and we make the two-run comparison part of the report rather than a robustness footnote - because "confidently arbitrary" is the failure mode that survives every within-run check and dies only at the second seed.**
- **Pattern:** **The paper pushes the identifiability question up one level, from the components to the *order* of the interaction, and states the synthesis that makes it crisp: a three-way product restricted to a support where one input equals another is exactly a two-way function, so the order cannot be recovered from that data.** On full-dimensional product support a genuinely k-way function cannot be written as a sum of lower-order terms and the order is identified; under rank-collapsed support it can, and between the extremes strong correlation degrades order identifiability well before complete collapse. The paper also makes its own headroom explicit in a way that matters for us: a hierarchical functional-ANOVA decomposition gives "the order of a dependence" a representation-independent definition, but only under extra regularity assumptions that full-dimensional support does not imply - and the gated model's listed modulators need a separate faithfulness assumption to bridge the structure to the parameters. Read against run 740 (26% of the target preserved, so the experiment was a boundary case) and run 742 (a partition exact by construction, so sum-of-parts and joint effect coincide): the recurrence is that **every "this is what the component means" claim rests on a bridge assumption that the headline theorem does not carry.** Mechanical rule for us: **whenever we claim an interaction of a particular order, we state the support condition that makes the order identifiable and the bridge assumption that makes the fitted parameters mean that structure, and we say which of the two is doing the work - because "the decomposition is unique" and "the fitted parameters are that decomposition" are separate theorems and the first is routinely reported as if it were the second.**

- **Pattern:** **This is the folder's cleanest demonstration that a net signed number has an *arbitrary zero*, and it arrives with a construction rather than an argument: on a synthetic function whose interesting coefficient sits behind a third-order interaction with zero expectation, the population one-dimensional partial dependence for that feature is identically zero, so every model's standard chart is flat while the effect is strong.** Only the paper's magnitude summary - the shared positive backbone, which cannot cancel by construction - retains the quadratic shape. Worse for the signed reading, in the unconstrained rank-1 alternative each individual factor is only identifiable up to a joint sign flip, so a fit exists in which the features' own curves look negative while the product is positive because four signs cancel. Read against run 742 (the signed gross/net budget, where a net of 0.05 could be a mechanism or an absence and only the pair distinguished them) and run 741 (attribution as a pair of estimands), the distinction is that those entries say a net hides its components, while this one shows a marginal operation erases a component outright and shows a quantity that survives. Mechanical rule for us: **every component score we publish carries a magnitude summary that is non-negative by construction alongside the signed one, the two are reported together, and we state which gauge fixed the sign - because a signed number whose zero point is set by a gauge choice is not a measurement, and a signed net whose components cancel to zero reads identically to a component that is absent.**
- **Pattern:** **The paper's principal stated limitation is that its own model is not identifiable, and it lists three distinct mechanisms - scaling and permutation, non-rectangular support, and noisy fitting - then shows that positivity fixes only the first two partially and that the third causes whole bags to converge to different factorisations of the same function.** The consequence is mechanical: some fitted bags are discarded rather than averaged, so only a fraction of the ensemble contributes, across-seed variance is high, and the recommended fix (aligning all bags on the positive rank-1 manifold) is left as future work. The paper states plainly that the latent factors should not be read as uniquely recoverable objects but as one admissible representation chosen by the fitting procedure. Read against run 744 (a decomposition whose *cost* is exponential in order) and run 743 (a remainder that is only ever measured, never bounded), the recurrence is that **every exact-looking decomposition in this folder arrives with a caveat about which of its parts are real** - and this is the first entry to catalogue the caveats as separate mechanisms with different fixes. Mechanical rule for us: **before we report any decomposed component as a fact about the model, we run the decomposition at no fewer than two seeds or two initialisations, align them in a named gauge, and report the between-run disagreement in the component values themselves - because two runs that fit equally well and disagree on a factor have produced two admissible representations, and reporting either of them alone as the structure is a statement about our optimiser, not about the network.** Cross-reference run 740 (a decomposition that preserved only 26% of the target and was labelled a boundary case).
- **Pattern:** **The cost boundary carried out of run 744 is crossed here, but in the direction the folder had not considered: the escape from exponential subset enumeration is not a cheaper exact decomposition, it is a *different function class* with a hard rank cap - and the paper's own benchmark shows the cap costing accuracy.** Training cost is stated as linear in stages, bagged grids, split iterations, samples and features, with the bagged grids embarrassingly parallel and histogram binning cutting the per-iteration sample dependence; but every stage contributes at most two products, so the model's separation rank is bounded at twice the stage count, and across 27 datasets the family's unconstrained version wins more aggregate rows than the positivity-constrained one the paper advocates. The approximation rate carries its own caveat: it is dimension-free only for a target class whose required order of mixed differentiability grows with the dimension. Read against run 742 (completeness by construction, where the sum of parts *is* the joint effect) and run 744 (exponential subset cost, left open), the distinction is that those entries ask whether a decomposition is exact and how much it costs, this one shows a cheap decomposition is available only by restricting the hypothesis class. Mechanical rule for us: **when we trade an exponential exact decomposition for a tractable one, we publish the rank or order cap that makes it tractable, the accuracy lost against the uncapped version at matched budget, and a sentence naming which function class the guarantee is for - because "scalable decomposition" and "exact decomposition" are answers to different questions, and the cap is the price that is never in the headline.**

- **Pattern:** **This is the answer to the compositionality carry, and the answer is an arithmetic guarantee rather than a learned correction: a contribution defined on full input-to-output path terms sums exactly to the output change at every granularity, so "sum of the parts" and "joint effect" are the same quantity by construction rather than by fit.** Hierarchical completeness holds for any family of subnetworks whose path sets partition a larger one, which makes neurons, edges, convolutional channels and arbitrary circuits all readable as marginals of a single path-level matrix, and recovers Integrated Gradients, neuron conductance and CODEC as special cases of one definition. Mechanical rule for us: **we do not fit a correction to close the gap between a sum of component scores and the measured group effect; we define our scores on units whose partition is exact, verify the partition sums to the measured output difference to within the printed numerical error, and report that error - because a decomposition that is complete by construction makes the sum-of-parts-versus-joint question disappear, and one that is incomplete by 74% cannot be repaired by any downstream model.** Cross-reference run 733 (a theorem predicting an ablation it then measured).

- **Pattern:** **Bulk patching lands on the diagonal against summed contributions while single-context patching does not sum correctly, and that asymmetry is the cleanest statement in the folder of why group interventions need group scores.** Averaged over 3,001 simulated contexts the path contribution tracks the patching effect closely, and the difference between them is much smaller than the spread across contexts, so the contribution behaves as an efficient summary of a distribution that is expensive to sample; but remove-one and keep-one patching each fail to sum to the output (the XOR toy model counts the product term twice under one convention and never under the other), and only complete contributions recover it. The paper also shows the search must be exact rather than heuristic: a beam search over the most important edges has to enumerate about 100 times more paths than requested to find the true top ones, and 100 times more again over neurons. Mechanical rule for us: **any group intervention we report is paired with the summed per-component score for the same group, the comparison is printed as a scatter against the diagonal rather than as a correlation, and where a cheap heuristic stands in for an exact search we report how much extra enumeration it costs to reach the exact answer - because a diagonal scatter says the score predicts the intervention and a correlation only says the two move together.**

- **Pattern:** **This is the folder's sharpest statement that an attribution is a *pair* of estimands, not a number, and that the gap between them is the measurement - arriving with a closed-form reason rather than a correlation.** Denoising and noising are not two recipes for one quantity: the paper proves the first estimates the pure indirect effect (bypass edges blocked) while the second estimates that effect *plus* a mediated interaction equal to the mixed second directional derivative of the downstream map in the two perturbation directions. So the gap is not estimator error to be reduced; it is a property of the model at that operating point. Read against run 740 (probe readout moved 0.24 while behaviour moved on ~6% of items) and run 739 (an exactly-scored influence whose Spearman dropped from 0.96 to 0.70 on the ViT), the recurrence is now three deep and the shape is identical: **two instruments aimed at the "same" causal quantity disagree, and the disagreement is the finding.** Mechanical rule for us: **every causal attribution we publish is reported as an ordered pair from both intervention directions on the same component, with the difference reported as its own quantity and the perturbation distance named - because a single-direction attribution silently adds a term whose size we do not know, and a term that is invisible at small patch distance becomes dominant at larger distances without any change to the model.** Cross-reference run 733 (an ablation that moved the measured geometry without moving AUROC in the predicted direction).
- **Pattern:** **The paper converts a nuisance into a free functional label, and that conversion is directly reusable: the *sign* of the interaction term sorts heads into three mechanistically distinct roles that neither estimator recovers alone.** Negative interaction with positive pure effect is backup compensation (the head's marginal contribution shrinks because a peer is doing the same job); positive interaction with near-zero pure effect is a context-specific mechanism whose whole contribution is realised only when the downstream circuit is intact; negative pure effect with positive interaction is a harmful mechanism partially opposed by its peers. The signs are consistent within functional groups, so clustering on the pair recovers the published labels without re-reading the circuit paper. Read against run 734 (eight collapse scalars used as covariates to pick a detector family) and run 737 (a coefficient swept to move collapse and behaviour together): those entries use a scalar as a *predictor*; this one uses a *signed difference* as a *classifier*, and the classifier's categories are causal roles rather than scores. Mechanical rule for us: **when a white-box statistic has two natural reference points (two directions, two baselines, two ablations), we compute the signed contrast and report it as a categorical variable with its role interpretation attached, rather than collapsing it into a magnitude - because the magnitude answers "how much" and the sign answers "what kind", and downstream analysis almost always needs the second.**
- **Pattern:** **The measured quantity depends on the experimental design choices the researcher makes, and three of the four sufficient conditions for it to vanish are choices - which makes "clean single-component attribution" a statement about the experiment, not the model.** The interaction term is provably zero when the component is unaffected by the input change, when the downstream map is locally affine, or when the two perturbations have no shared component in the curved directions; and empirically it is small exactly for semantically close prompt pairs, for single-word counterfactuals, and for piecewise-affine compiled models. The paper states the consequence plainly: the magnitude of the phenomenon is set by the evaluation conditions rather than by the circuit, and benchmark suites built on compiled transformers cannot exhibit it at all. - **Pattern:** **The folder now has the answer to the open-set half of the collapse question, and it is a warning rather than a tool: a classifier vector with zero training samples behind it is not idle, it converges to a specific direction with the same confidence and the same tiny variance as a trained one.** Theorems 2 and 3 say that with K₁ populated classes and K−K₁ empty ones, the empty vectors all coincide and point along minus the global feature mean, orthogonal to the trained weights; empirically they reach about 0.999-1.000 mutual similarity by epoch 50, i.e. *before* the known classes have settled. Read against run 734 (self-duality and weight equiangularity carry the OOD-detector prediction, so the head rather than the feature cloud is the object of interest) and run 733 (compaction moved the spread ratio without moving AUROC in the direction theory wanted), the distinction is now usable: those entries argued that head geometry matters; this one says head geometry is *generated* by support, and where support is zero the geometry is generated by something else entirely. Mechanical rule for us: **when we read prototypes or classifier rows out of a model and treat a low-support or zero-support direction as "unused", we first measure the gram matrix among such directions and their angle to the global feature mean - because the theory here says empty directions collapse onto one another and look as crisp as trained ones, and a crispness statistic computed without checking for that collapse cannot tell a real class from a placeholder.**
- **Pattern:** **The load-bearing variable is the loss's normalisation, and the paper's whole result is that changing it from per-sample to per-class is what converts a distorted geometry into the standard one - which makes normalisation a confound in every cross-model geometry comparison the folder has run.** Per-class averaging is algebraically inverse-frequency weighting, and at IF=100 the globally averaged objective prints class frequency straight into the similarity matrix (off-diagonals grading from about −0.3 in the head classes to about 0.1 in the tail, a span of roughly 0.4) while the class-wise version stays inside a band under 0.024. The BCE bias is the cleanest confirmation available in this literature: 4.663-4.669 measured against 4.6698 predicted on CIFAR10-LT across four imbalance factors, and 6.328-6.332 against 6.3437 on CIFAR100-LT, on two architectures - agreement that a free parameter cannot fake. Compare run 731 (a bound repaired by adding a reciprocal-density term) and run 732 (a score whose tuned k degenerated to 1): three entries now in which the difference between two configurations is a single algebraic term in the objective rather than an architectural or data choice. Mechanical rule for us: **any claim we make that two checkpoints differ in geometry, collapse, or prototype quality carries the loss normalisation of each, and where the normalisations differ we treat the geometry difference as attributable to the loss until a matched-normalisation comparison says otherwise - because per-class and per-sample averaging are the same architecture with different objectives, and no measured similarity can distinguish them afterwards.**
- **Pattern:** **The one prediction the paper reports failing is a conditioning failure rather than a refutation, and it is the folder's cleanest example of a theorem whose residual is numerical - the score you want is a direction of a vector whose norm is going to zero.** The empty-class vector should sit exactly antiparallel to the global feature mean, and at the theoretical minimum it does; but as the mean norm collapses toward zero any perturbation reorients it, so the measured cosine wanders (−0.6181 for BCE at epoch 600, and −0.2504 → −0.0492 → −0.0442 across CE stages in Table 3) while every other statistic in the same table is within noise of its constant. The paper states the cause plainly and leaves the quantity in the table rather than dropping it. Read against run 729 (a correlation computed on surviving seeds) and run 727 (a score whose invariance group was proved before its diagnostic value was claimed): the difference is that those papers' numbers were compromised by which samples survived, while this number is compromised by the arithmetic of a normalised angle near the origin. Mechanical rule for us: **a normalised direction or cosine statistic we publish is accompanied by the norm of the vector it was computed from, and where that norm falls below the scale at which the direction is stable we report the instability rather than the angle - because a ratio of two small quantities is a measurement of noise, and an error term that is a conditioning problem is fixed by changing the statistic, not by adding data.**

- **Pattern:** **This is the folder's first entry where a purely checkpoint-derived geometric measurement predicts a held-out outcome with no fitted behavioural coefficient - and the paper's own random-shortlist control removes most of the credit at exactly the scale where the folder has been asking for prediction.** The instrument is the eight Neural Collapse scalars, all computable from training data alone, and the outcome is which of 22 detectors lands in a statistically indistinguishable top clique; inside the CNN family it works (55-80% regret reduction, 65 of 66 comparisons), and on 47 ImageNet models a **random shortlist of the same cardinality reaches 1.25 against the predictor's 1.05**, significant under the rank test and not under the mean test, while on 40 self-supervised probes it loses outright at far shift (8.08 against 0.85 for Maha++). Read against run 731 (a per-sample bound scored on held-out data, with validation-only hyperparameters) and run 730 (a negative result repaired by measuring whether the phenomenon was expressible), the distinction is now sharp and reusable: **a representation-side statistic can be validated in the aggregate — does it rank models the way behaviour ranks them — without being validated as a cause, and the control that separates those two is a random draw of matched size, not a stronger baseline.** Mechanical rule for us: **every selector, router or probe-set we publish that is derived from white-box statistics is scored against a random draw of the same cardinality in the same table, and we report which of the two tests it passes (rank test or mean-difference test), because a predictor that contains the oracle 57% of the time against 37% expected by chance can still be beaten by chance once eight near-tied candidates exist.**
- **Pattern:** **The collapse geometry that carries the prediction is not the spread ratio the folder has been chasing — self-duality and the equiangularity of the classifier weights are, which moves the object of interest from the features to the linear head.** The within/between covariance ratio is measured and printed (VGG-13 around 0.002-0.010 against roughly 0.012-0.037 for the ViT) but it is one of eight covariates, and the strongest single metric is the maximal equiangularity of the classifier weights in three of four strata (0.68-0.77, and 0.88 for the equiangularity of the weights in the weakest stratum). The coefficient signs say the same thing from the other direction: CTM is favoured when the representation is collapsed *and* self-dual (negative on both), while fDBD is favoured precisely when the weights do **not** align with the class means (positive on self-duality), i.e. the two most-recommended feature-side detectors divide on a property of the head, not of the feature cloud. Note the ViT explanation the paper offers in Appendix B.4 — pretrained residuals mean OOD inputs land inside subspaces created during pretraining, so class-conditional PCA filtering is the only intervention that helps ViTs, and global projection is the only one that helps CNNs. Read against run 733 (a compaction ablation that moved the spread ratio without moving the AUROC in the direction the theory wanted) and run 732 (a density score whose tuned optimum degenerated to a single neighbour): **the folder's geometric covariates are turning out to be properties of the readout rather than of the representation.** Mechanical rule for us: **when we attribute a reliability or interpretability effect to feature geometry we regress it against the head-geometry terms (self-duality, weight equiangularity) as well, and if those absorb the effect we say the finding is about the classifier rather than the representation — because a collapsed feature cloud with a misaligned head behaves nothing like a collapsed cloud with a self-dual one, and only one of those is a claim about the model's inner state.**
- **Pattern:** **The prior-shift result this entry supplies closes the folder's near-shift thread in the negative: geometry-derived scores carry no information about near distribution shift, and the failure is now replicated across three independent instruments with chance-level numbers in the same table.** Run 732's embedding-density score sat at 0.5867 AUROC on its internal near-shift set with Energy 0.5858, Mahalanobis 0.5850 and ODIN 0.5878 — all at chance — and here the whole detector-family analysis is built on near/mid/far stratification because the near regime is where the transitions are least decisive (near-OOD on CNNs is dominated by Energy and MLS, which read the logits; the geometry-aware detectors only take over at mid and far). Note also that the paper's own three-group stratification is argued for on the grounds that a binary near/far split hides the mid-OOD winners (a ViT far clique of 8 CSFs collapsing into a focused KPCA-RecError mid clique and a distinct Residual/ViM far clique). Read against run 725 (a bound whose failing constant was estimated rather than argued away) and run 723 (a rank at a fixed variance cut measuring the measurement): **the reason near-shift geometry fails is that near-shift OOD inputs sit in the same region of feature space as in-distribution inputs, so every statistic that summarises that region — density, distance, boundary count, NC metric — returns the same value for both.** Mechanical rule for us: **a near-shift claim is our test set's hardest case and gets its own row in every table, reported at chance when it is at chance, and we never average a near-shift cell into a headline that is dominated by far-shift rows — because the aggregate that includes far shift is the aggregate where geometry-derived scores look useful.**

- **Pattern:** **This is the first paper in the folder whose "explanation" is a per-sample predictive bound that is actually scored against a held-out behaviour - and it gets there by repairing a bound instead of replacing it, which is the cheapest move in the arc.** The textbook per-region Hoeffding bound (their Eq. 4) is finite only when a region holds training samples; in a deep net almost every test input lands in a region holding none, so the bound is literally infinite and unusable for ranking. Instead of abandoning the partition, they smooth the empirical error across neighbouring subfunctions with a Gaussian kernel in Hamming distance between activation patterns, which makes the bound finite everywhere and leaves a two-term score: weighted neighbour error plus 1/P(h_i), the reciprocal of local training density. Read against run 730 (where the negative result was repaired by measuring whether the phenomenon was expressible at all) and run 725 (a bound whose failing constant was estimated rather than argued away), the discipline is now explicit in three consecutive runs: **when a published bound is infinite, undefined or inconsistent in the regime that matters, the repair is the contribution, and the repair has to be visible in the score's algebra.** Mechanical rule for us: **every bound or score we publish is written in the form (fit term) + (uncertainty term) with the uncertainty term named as a function of local sample density, and we report its value at the specific test inputs where our evaluation set has no support - because a bound that returns infinity on five percent of the data is a bound that has silently decided those samples do not exist, and the density reciprocal is the term that keeps them in the ranking.** Cross-reference run 726 (a control curve that separated reorganisation from flattening), run 722 (an invariance number whose arithmetic, not its geometry, produced the finding).
- **Pattern:** **A metric that is the best on average and best in only two of four categories is reported here as a per-category *difference from the winner*, which is the honest table shape - and it also removes the reader's ability to see the cells where the method loses, which the appendix then quietly contains.** Table 1 gives only the deficit to the top method per architecture x dataset (-0.007 for theirs, -0.014 for entropy, -0.181 for the GP), so the headline reads as dominance; the absolute tables are in Appendix C-D, where ResNet50-CIFAR100 in-distribution AUROC is 0.827 against entropy's 0.859 and cluster distance edges theirs 0.754 to 0.750 on one OOD cell. The abstract's "up to 20% absolute" is the CIFAR100 effective-accuracy best case (70-73% -> 90-92%) standing next to a roughly 7-point CIFAR10 gain that the same sentence does not distinguish. Read against run 721 (six prose/table disagreements in one paper), run 720 (a multiplier quoted as 2,000x and 1,300x), run 722 (PC1 given as 68-83% in one section and 70-94% in another): the recurring shape is a summary statistic whose aggregation level hides the dispersion. Mechanical rule for us: **a comparison table we publish carries the absolute numbers for every method in every cell, and any "difference from the best" summary is printed beside the absolute table rather than instead of it - because a deficit average is a mean over cells, and a mean over four cells can be negative while a third of the cells are losses, which is exactly the margin that decides whether a practitioner adopts the tool.** Cross-reference run 729 (a correlation computed on the surviving seed subset), run 723 (five contributions, four unmeasured).
- **Pattern:** **The theoretical machinery generalises past its own paper: completeness of the bit space turns two exponential sums over activation patterns into O(M) and O(N^2 + M^3) with binomial shell counts, and that is the same Hamming-shell identity every walk-based geometric statistic in this arc needs to be tractable.** Because every pattern at Hamming distance b from a fixed pattern contributes the same kernel value, the normaliser does not depend on which pattern you are normalising (Eq. 35-36), and the double sum over the full bit space collapses to a look-up table indexed by the Hamming distance between two observed patterns, built by iterating shells and choosing which flips move toward versus away from the target (Eq. 40). Deep networks are saved from an intractable partition only by assuming the *full* bit space - which is precisely the idealisation that assigns density to unreachable regions and that the authors list as a limitation. Read against run 728 (LC computed by one forward pass over a sampled hull) and run 729 (folding by a walk whose bit gaps exceed one in deep layers), the shared constraint is now clear: every cheap partition statistic in this folder is bought by pretending the feasible pattern set is the whole bit cube. Mechanical rule for us: **when we adopt a cheap partition or walk statistic we state which idealisation purchased the cheapness - full bit space instead of the feasible set, last layer only, sampled hull instead of the region - and we measure the error that idealisation introduces at least once, because the exponential-to-polynomial trick here is valid exactly when the reachable set is the cube, and the paper's own numbers are then a lower bound rather than an estimate.** Cross-reference run 727 (an extension whose lost structure the authors named in the same paragraph), run 725 (bias-only noise as the perturbation that keeps the geometry).

- **Pattern:** **The paper's real instrument is an arithmetic identity that dismantles a composite score everyone had been quoting, and it is the folder's cheapest example of a score whose two factors must travel together - judge-verified frequency difference factors exactly as frequency times (twice accuracy minus one), so a hypothesis that fires on a tenth of inputs and is always right and one that fires on all inputs and is right 55% of the time both read 0.1.** Appendix B.1 derives it and then makes the point with those two hypotheses side by side. Mechanical rule for us: **before we publish any aggregate score for a probe, feature or explanation, we factor it into a rate of application and a rate of correctness and show the algebra that produced it - and where the product cannot be split, we say so - because a single number that multiplies how often a claim applies by how well it discriminates cannot be used to choose between a narrow true claim and a broad useless one, and the choice between those two is the entire design question for a white-box model that has to say when it applies.** Cross-reference run 722 (an invariance number whose absolute size said nothing and whose ratio held the finding), run 728 (a control curve that separated "reorganised" from "flattened" by computing the same statistic at three probe sets).

- **Pattern:** **The paper's one genuinely exact result is a theorem that confines folding to depth two or more, and its proof doubles as the cleanest re-derivation of why one hidden layer cannot separate XOR - geometry from a theorem rather than from a dataset.** Lemma 1 asserts convexity of a union of activation regions is equivalent to Hamming convexity of the bit patterns, and the forward direction is just the observation that crossing a whole-space hyperplane flips exactly one bit, so a straight segment is a shortest Hamming path; the reverse direction says a convex bit set forces the corresponding region union to be convex. The load-bearing hypothesis is *whole-space hyperplane* - first-layer neurons only - and the authors state the cost in the same section: deeper layers produce adjacent regions whose patterns differ by more than one bit, which is precisely what Example 2 exhibits on CantorNet. Compare run 727 (an extension whose lost structure the authors named in the same paragraph: the same discipline), run 718 (a framework whose five contributions included one theorem and four claims), run 724 (an exact re-description yielding zero measured numbers - the benign version of the same shape). Mechanical rule for us: **we separate a statistic's range and invariances from its predictive content in separate sentences, we let boundedness license comparison across models and nothing else, and we never let a normalised score stand in for a mechanism - because [0,1] is a scale, not a finding, and the denominator that produces it (total Hamming distance walked) moves whenever the walk's step count or step rule moves.** Cross-reference run 722 (a residual fraction whose invariance followed from dimension, not dynamics), run 723 (rho_exec/rho_rand, where the ratio was the finding and the invariance was noise).

- **Pattern:** **The cheapest partition statistic in this folder's reach is a hyperplane-cut count over a sampled hull, and this paper is where the random-probe control was introduced - which makes it the origin of the control that runs 723-727 each re-derived independently.** Around a probe point the authors draw P orthonormal offsets, push the hull's vertices through in one forward pass, and count per layer how many pre-activations change sign across the vertices; no labels, no loss, no task, and it reproduces the doubly-descending curve that an exact region-count method (SplineCAM) gives on the same MLP. Read against run 726 (the three-probe-set rule credited to a 2024 paper) and run 725 (bias-perturbed boundary density averaged over the data distribution), the lineage is now visible: the random-point curve is not an innovation of the later papers, it is already here, plotted as a third colour beside train and test and doing exactly the job it does later - separating "the partition reorganised near the data" from "the partition changed everywhere", since the train-side ascent does not appear at random points. Mechanical rule for us: **when we adopt a control from a paper we cite the paper that introduced it rather than the one that restated it, and any locality claim we make is accompanied by the random-point version of the same statistic computed on the same checkpoints - because the random curve is what turns "the model uses dense regions near the data" into a falsifiable statement about where the boundaries are.** Cross-reference run 726 (LC at data, shifted and random probes), run 727 (invariance group stated before a statistic is used).
- **Pattern:** **The same manipulation moves the phenomenon in opposite directions across two architectures inside this one paper, and the authors report both - so the trajectory is the finding and the direction of every effect is a per-setting fact.** Depth reduces the ascent peak and the train-test LC gap on MNIST MLPs, but under induced grokking depth raises the ascent peak and delays generalisation; on CIFAR10 CNNs depth raises the ascent peak and train-test LC are nearly indistinguishable throughout, where on MNIST the ascent is almost entirely a training-set effect. Width is non-monotone even within one setting: climbing 20 to 1000 starts the ascent earlier and higher, and 2000 lowers the peak again. Two regularisers that both "remove the final descent" do so with opposite side effects - batch norm raises LC on train, test and random points, weight decay lowers the ascent peak and shortens it. This is the honest shape of a phenomenon paper and it is citable precisely because the disagreement is printed: the three-phase shape survives every sweep while every specific direction flips at least once. Mechanical rule for us: **we distinguish, in our own write-up and in every entry we cite, a shape claim from a direction claim - a shape that survives N settings is evidence, a direction observed in one setting is a hypothesis - and where an architecture family changes the direction we report the two families side by side rather than averaging them, because a mechanism whose sign depends on the architecture is a mechanism that depends on something not yet named.** Cross-reference run 722 (three spectral objects in one paper telling three different stories), run 721 (six prose/table disagreements in one paper), run 727 (a score whose invariance group decided what it could be compared with).
- **Pattern:** **The migration story is carried by pictures plus a handful of slice counts, and the paper's own conclusion concedes there is no theory - which places the whole arc's central object on the demonstration side of the line, again.** Exact partition visualisations on 2-D slices through three training samples show boundaries crowding onto training points during the ascent and moving to the decision boundary during the second descent; the quantitative support is the LC curve and exact counts on select slices, never a boundary-distance distribution over the input distribution. The Conclusion states that the phases remain unexplained and that the work rebuts earlier stationary-partition assumptions without offering a replacement model. Compare run 724 (an exact re-description that measured nothing), run 726 (region counts on four selected slices standing in for a distribution), run 723 (four of five contributions claimed rather than measured): four papers in this arc now describe the same migration and none measures where the boundaries go as a distribution. - **Pattern:** **The paper's real instrument is not the folding score - it is the order in which it checks that score: invariances first, diagnostic value never - and that order is the cheapest control in the folder's reach.** Before anyone is invited to use chi, they prove four things about it: extra samples inside one region do not move it (Prop. 4.1), so it depends on which regions a walk visits and not on the sampling density; chi = 0 has an exact iff-characterisation (Prop. 4.2); the score is direction-sensitive with a three-bit counterexample (Remark 4.3) while flatness is not (Cor. 4.4); and the score is neither sub- nor super-additive (Eq. 4, Eq. 5). Read against the folder's standing complaint - run 722's projection fraction whose absolute value was tiny and whose finding lived entirely in the ratio, run 723's r90 at one variance cut with no spectrum, run 725's rank_eps monotone in eps by construction - this is the same discipline applied one step earlier: those papers established what their numbers were *relative to* only after reporting them. A scalar does not get to be an explanation until its invariance group is known, because an invariant quantity is comparable across models and a non-invariant one is comparable only across the samples that produced it. Mechanical rule for us: **for every statistic we publish in the white-box model we state its invariance group explicitly - under repeated sampling inside one region, under reversal of the path or order, under decomposition into sub-paths - and where we cannot prove invariance we measure it on our own data and report the spread, because a statistic is only a comparison device and a statistic whose invariances are unknown cannot be compared with anything.** Cross-reference run 724 (an exact re-description whose authors measured nothing - the same shape, differently resolved), run 719 (a correction term that loses to the simple score at the window sizes practitioners use - an invariance question asked about a correction rather than about a base statistic).
- **Pattern:** **The extension beyond ReLU is argued from a definition rather than tested, and the argument is the part worth keeping: a linear region is nothing but an equivalence class of inputs with identical binarised activations, so the partition survives any monotone activation even after it stops being a partition into affine pieces.** Def. 4.5 defines x ~ y iff their binarised patterns are Hamming-identical, checks the three equivalence axioms in three sentences, and then notes the honest cost of the move in the same breath: "we lose the geometrical interpretation of equivalence classes as linear regions." What survives is exactly what the folding measure needs - a discrete walk through a set of classes with distances between them - and what is lost is every geometric claim made about those classes, so the beta-parameter and the region-count literature silently do not transfer. Compare run 723 (five contributions, four unmeasured), run 721 (six prose/table disagreements): this paper is the clean case where the authors state what the generalisation costs them instead of carrying the old vocabulary across. Mechanical rule for us: **when we extend an object to a wider class of models we name, in the same paragraph, the structure that the extension does not preserve - because a definition that survives a generalisation is not the same object, and an invariant we computed on the narrower class is not automatically an invariant of the wider one.**
- **Pattern:** **Every empirical fact in this paper is inherited from a companion it cites without an identifier, and the paper says so plainly - which makes it the folder's clearest example of a theory paper whose theory rests on someone else's measurement.** The depth-dependence, the low-error/high-folding association and the near-invariance of folding to width (60- vs 600-neuron nets at fixed depth) all trace to "On Space Folds of ReLU Neural Networks" (TMLR 2025), cited by author-year with no arXiv id; the only experiment run here is a Mann-Whitney comparison of intra- vs inter-class medians, reported as significant with the threshold deferred to Cohen's conventions and no number given. The regulariser proposed in §6 is described as "untested" in §7. This is the benign version of run 726's shape (a paper whose headline was measured with a different instrument than the theory described): here the authors segregate what they proved from what they borrowed. Mechanical rule for us: **before quoting a paper's empirical claim we trace it one hop - if the number lives in a cited companion, the citation is to the companion and the entry says "reported in <paper>, not re-measured here" - because a two-hop citation chain is where the instrument, the sample size and the caveats all quietly drop out.** Cross-reference run 713 (numbers inherited from a survey and never re-measured), run 726 (a drop measured with a different instrument than the bound written for it).

- **Pattern:** **The control that makes this paper's headline falsifiable is a curve nobody else in the folder plots - local complexity probed at uniformly random points - and it is the reason a "complexity dropped" claim here cannot be confused with a global decay.** During the second descent, LC around training, test *and* random points all fall; if only the data curves moved, the paper's story would be indistinguishable from the network simply smoothing everywhere, which is exactly the failure mode that makes run 723's r90 and run 722's rho≈1.000 unreadable. The random-probe curve forces the claim into its real form: boundaries leave the data neighbourhoods and concentrate somewhere the random probes do not sample, which is then verified on the slice. Note the cost - 1,000 ResNet18 probes in about 28 s on an RTX 8000 - so this control is cheap enough to be mandatory rather than aspirational. Mechanical rule for us: **every locality statistic we report (boundary density, region count, curvature, rank) is reported at three probe sets - the data, a distribution-shifted set, and uniformly random points - because a statistic computed only at the data cannot distinguish "the model reorganised" from "the model flattened", and the random set is the null that separates them.** Cross-reference run 725 (bias-perturbed boundary density weighted by the data distribution), run 722 (a residual fraction whose only informative form was its ratio to a random basis), run 714 (a spread statistic whose value was set by the random-initialisation baseline).
- **Pattern:** **The paper's own diagnostic for whether its measure is valid is the most portable instrument in it, and it is a test of the neighbourhood rather than of the network: push the probe polytope through the layers and measure how much its shape deforms.** Graph eccentricity and diameter of the polytope rise roughly exponentially with depth for larger radii and stay flat below about 0.014 on CIFAR10 and for the ResNet18, which is why the radii used are 0.005 and 1e-4 rather than something more local; and even then the authors report that the LC *dynamics* are similar across large and small radii, so the qualitative curve survives the approximation even where the absolute value does not. This is the first entry in the folder that pays for a hyperparameter with a measurement instead of asserting it, and the same operation is what ordinary probing lacks: a linear probe never checks whether the representation neighbourhood it is reading still corresponds to an input neighbourhood. Mechanical rule for us: **any statistic computed on a pushed-forward neighbourhood (a polytope, a ball, a patch of activation space) ships with the deformation of that neighbourhood measured at the depth it was taken, and the radius is chosen as the largest one where deformation is still flat - because a local statistic taken through a deep network is a statement about an object that may no longer be local by the time you read it.**
- **Pattern:** **Region counting and circuit counting are the same measurement here, and the paper says the identity out loud - a region is one active-neuron configuration, adjacent regions differ by one neuron, so boundary density around a point *is* circuit-transition density around that point.** That single sentence collapses two literatures this folder has been reading separately (the spline/partition line from runs 718, 723-725 and the mechanistic circuit line), and it comes with the empirical claim that circuits are exhausted rather than accumulated late in training: the partition coarsens around data and concentrates on the boundary, so the number of distinct subgraphs traversed in a data locality collapses, most sharply in the deeper layers. The load-bearing caveat is that the paper's own theory stops before this: it offers no account of why the migration happens only after interpolation, and the association between migration and robustness is never tested by moving boundaries artificially. Mechanical rule for us: **when we write that a feature or circuit "is used", we state the measure as a density over an input locality and report how that density changes over training, and we treat a dense-region count and a circuit count as one statistic rather than two corroborations - because counting regions and counting circuits from the same partition is one measurement, and two names for one number is not evidence.**

- **Pattern:** **The paper's real contribution is a definition that makes the partition object answerable to the data distribution, and the trick that buys it is perturbing biases only - which is the missing half of every partition statistic this folder has been computing.** Counting regions at fixed weights needs a parametric solve; averaging the boundary density over Gaussian *bias* noise needs only a co-area formula, and bias noise translates boundaries without rotating them, so the averaged object is still the same geometry (their sigma ablation at 0.025/0.05/0.1 and the bias-vs-bias+weight comparison in Appendix B.1 both leave the picture qualitatively unchanged). Theorem 2 then factorises that density into a per-neuron term, ‖∇z_i(x)‖ × ρ_b(z_i(x)) × 1{z_i good at x}, i.e. gradient norm times a threshold-crossing weight times a liveness indicator. Read against run 724 (the radius dropped from the power-diagram object, so a centroid can name a tile the input does not occupy) and run 723 (a rank at a fixed 90% variance cut measuring the measurement), this is the third consecutive run arriving at the same structural point from a different direction: a geometric quantity computed in ambient space is not a statement about the network until it is weighted by where the data is. Mechanical rule for us: **every partition, region, curvature or boundary statistic we report is averaged over a data distribution (or an explicit input sample) rather than over input space, is computed under a perturbation that moves boundaries without re-orienting them (bias noise), and is reported per neuron as gradient-norm times threshold-crossing so the contribution can be attributed - because a region count in ℝ^D upper-bounds nothing about behaviour, and a boundary density near the data is the only version of the object that a mechanism could act through.**
- **Pattern:** **The one place the paper's own bound fails, it diagnoses the failure by measuring a constant inside the bound instead of softening the claim - and calls the result unexpected rather than rescued; this is the template the folder should copy for every relation it publishes.** Total variation and local complexity drop together on MNIST at 2× He initialization, which is the setting they chose; at standard He initialization the correlation "seems to break down", and at 3× the picture changes again (Appendix B.3, Figure 8). Rather than hedge, they estimate the bound's own Lipschitz term as the max over layers of the suffix matrix-product operator norm, show the corrected lower bound resumes tracking LC across 88 repeated runs (Figure 9), and then state that the late-training TV *spike* is attributable to growing Lipschitz constants and "merits further investigation" - an inconclusive diagnosis reported as inconclusive. Note against run 721 (six prose/table disagreements where the reversed ordering supported the thesis) and run 722 (an invariance number the author himself called nearly contentless): those authors reported the doubtful number; this one reported the ablation that broke it. Mechanical rule for us: **when a predicted relation fails under our own ablation, we do not drop the ablation from the write-up - we estimate the constant that could absorb the discrepancy, re-test with that estimate, and state plainly whether the estimate rescued the bound or whether the residual is unexplained; because a bound with unmeasured constants is untestable in the regime where it matters, and the only honest outcome is a named residual.**
- **Pattern:** **Local rank is defined here as `rank_ε` - a count of singular values above a threshold - and the theory's relation to local complexity runs through that ε twice, which is an independent theoretical confirmation of the folder's empirical complaint about r90.** Theorem 5 bounds LC above by Σ_l √(C²·LR^ε_l + ε²n_l) and bounds Σ_l LR^ε_l above by (LC + error terms)/(c·ε²); both directions carry the threshold explicitly, and the exact-rank corollary only survives in the limit ε→0 through a weaker √LR form. Also worth holding: the paper's own Figure 12 shows local-rank dynamics on MNIST can be considerably more complex than on the synthetic task, and their Figure 2 correlation numbers (0.852 / 0.957 / 0.985 at layers 2/3/4) come from a 100-dimensional Gaussian-to-Gaussian regression with a randomly drawn cross-covariance, i.e. from the one setting where a low-rank target is known to exist. Read against run 723 (r90 at a fixed 90% variance cut with no null and no spectrum) and run 719 (a null the same paper had already shown to be wrong by orders of magnitude), this closes the loop from the theory side. Mechanical rule for us: **when we quote a rank we state ε (or the variance cut) and the spectrum it was cut from, we report the rank at two thresholds, and we never present a rank correlation obtained on a synthetic low-rank target as evidence about the rank of a trained network's features - because rank_ε is monotone in ε by definition, and a correlation between two thresholded quantities is partly a correlation between two thresholds.**

- **Pattern:** **This is the analytical parent of run 710's empirical paper, and reading it dissolves the distinction that four earlier runs were groping for: the "spectral edge" and the optimiser's coherent direction are not the same object, they are the *subspace* and its *basis*.** Run 717 found that a parameter-space diagnostic subspace was interchangeable with random directions of the same rank; run 718 found the general geometric object (a centroid of an affine tile) that the whole programme is a probe of; this paper supplies the skeleton both were standing inside - a dominant block of k* modes separated from a subdominant block by one gap, with the entire dynamic content in the gap size. The load-bearing move is that "signal versus noise" is the wrong axis in this regime. With p/W around ten million the classical Baik–Ben Arous–Péché threshold sits orders of magnitude below the weakest mode, so every mode is signal and the interesting boundary is between committed and wandering signal. For us this is the correct frame for reading weights: our problem is not detecting directions, it is telling the directions the network has settled on from the ones it is merely passing through. Mechanical rule for us: **report any spectrum-derived statement with its aspect ratio and with the position index at which it was taken, and never quote a signal/noise separation that came from an isotropic null without also reporting the empirical spread of the noise modes in the same window** - because when the null is off by two orders of magnitude, as run 710 already measured, the null is describing a different problem.
- **Pattern:** **The paper's most portable instrument is a stability coefficient computed by splitting the window in half, and its most instructive result is that the instrument loses to its own simplest component at the window sizes a practitioner would actually use.** The coefficient is one minus the ratio of window perturbation to squared gap, floored at zero, and it needs no Hessians and no gradients - just the spectrum. It is what makes "how reliably is this direction held" a number. But the causal sweep (§28) reports rank correlation 0.21 and 0.42 at windows of 10 and 20 checkpoints against 0.76 and 0.72 for the plain gradient product, crossing over only at 30 (0.75 versus 0.63) and 40 (0.68 versus 0.35). The paper reads the crossover as the minimum window for resolving subdominant modes and that is probably right; the consequence it does not draw is that most published trajectory analyses use windows of ten to twenty. Compare run 711 (a percentile statistic stable where a maximum swung two orders of magnitude, visible only because both were tabulated) and run 718 (a surrogate graded by recovering a single known answer). Mechanical rule for us: **a correction term added to a simple score is reported with the simple score's value alongside it at every setting we actually used, and the claim "the correction helps" is only made above the crossover point where it demonstrably does - because a two-parameter refinement that wins at a window size nobody chose a priori is a refinement tuned by the sweep.**
- **Pattern:** **The control design here is a hyperparameter contrast dressed as a mechanism test, and the paper is honest enough in its phrasing that the gap shows.** The headline is 24/24 grokking runs with weight decay against 1/24 without, with the sub-leading gap compressing 33-43x at the grokking step. But weight decay simultaneously changes the spectrum, the loss trajectory, the weight norms and whether the model memorises at all; no run manipulates the gap directly. The author's own wording - weight decay as a driver "by which" the dynamics are associated with generalisation - concedes the association. Meanwhile the one test that does intervene, removing a signal direction from the updates and comparing against the predicted per-direction loss change (§28), is the one that came back window-limited, and the one prediction that came back null (gap-flow sign correlation r = +0.08, R² = 0.006) is excused by the equation having three terms rather than retested. - **Done:** arxiv-2604.11962 - The Linear Centroids Hypothesis: How Deep Network Features Represent Data (read full text v1: abstract, §1-§5 including Discussion, Limitations, Impact Statement and Acknowledgments; Appendices A-H including the formal theory, the polygon/GELU replications, MNIST, the Platonic-representation check and the compute table; displayed maths read from the TeX pass; Figures 1-17 read from captions and reporting prose, not inspected as images; reference list read in full)
- **Pattern:** **This is the first entry in the folder that relocates the feature from the layer's output space to its *input* space and gets a falsifiable prediction out of the move - and the prediction is a dissociation, which is worth more to us than any accuracy gain it reports.** Because a centroid is the Jacobian of a sub-component summed over output dimensions (`J^T·1`), it describes what the local affine map *does*, whereas a latent activation describes only *where the input landed*. The paper's load-bearing experiment follows directly: inject colour into FashionMNIST at a swept correlation with the label, then probe colour linearly from latents and from centroids. Latents stay linearly decodable for colour even at random correlation; centroids are decodable only to the extent the label depends on colour. That is a claimed criterion for spuriousness - present-but-unused versus used - and it is the first operational test this folder holds for the distinction every "spurious feature" warning since run 690 has gestured at. Caveat that must travel with it: the evidence is a left-hand panel of a figure with no tabulated effect size and no seed spread, so the dissociation is demonstrated in kind, not in magnitude. Mechanical rule for us: **for every feature we report, we report both readings - the representation-side one (is it linearly decodable from activations?) and the action-side one (does removing or perturbing it move the output map?) - and we call a feature spurious only when the first is positive and the second is flat, because a direction being present is not the same as a direction being used, and only a pair of readings can separate them.** Cross-reference run 717 (a diagnostic subspace interchangeable with random of the same rank - the same "presence is not use" failure, met from the causal side), run 695 (a construction baseline making a score interpretable).
- **Pattern:** **An attribution score computed as a mean relative displacement over a neighbourhood is an intervention-shaped quantity obtained without running the intervention, and this folder now has the clean statement of what such a surrogate buys and what it does not.** Ablating one neuron and measuring the relative change in the sample's centroid, then averaging over a 256-point ball of radius 0.25 around the input embedding, ranks the previously published "an"-neuron of GPT2-Large in the top 99.8th percentile of its layer at layer 31 - a filter that avoids sweeping every neuron, arrived at from one prompt. Two properties are checked (low variance across draws, stable percentile across neighbourhood sizes) and one is not: the score is never validated against the ablation it stands for. So the claim "this ranking matches what ablation would find" rests on one recovered known answer, i.e. a test on the training case. Compare run 696 (a shuffled-community null beating every activation-only score) and run 717 (a 648x coupling ratio falling monotonically to 140 as the estimator is made less trivial) - both are cases where a surrogate was graded against itself. Mechanical rule for us: **any cheap surrogate for an expensive intervention (a gradient-based attribution, a centroid displacement, a Jacobian norm) is graded by rank correlation against the expensive intervention on a held-out set of at least dozens of cases, reported as a scatter and a Spearman value, and a surrogate validated only by recovering a single known answer is described as "consistent with" rather than "predicts".** Cross-reference run 694 (the one-forward-pass screen, first column only), run 696 (the shuffled null), run 717 (the degenerate-estimator limit).
- **Pattern:** **A paper whose every result is the shape of a plot is asking the reader to accept a method on one reading of its geometry - and the giveaway here is that the alternative hypothesis is criticised for exactly that.** The LRH is faulted for directions that are "linear even when the feature is spurious", yet the LCH evidence is PCA scatters, probe-accuracy curves, an 8-neighbour image grid and saliency images; the numbers that would settle it (probe accuracy, firing frequency, the cosine-similarity distributions whose bimodality at 0.4 carries the Platonic-representation argument) live only inside panels. The one quantity actually tabulated is compute cost - and it is not uniformly small: 8.7s versus 7.8s for DINO extraction, 881 versus 771 on MNIST, but 2329 versus 470 (about 5x) for the Llama-3.1-8B probes. Compare run 712 (a percentile threshold stable where a maximum swings two orders of magnitude, because both were tabulated) and run 715 (a circuit necessary in one seed, inert in another, only visible because both seeds were reported). Mechanical rule for us: **when we adopt a representation for our own probes we adopt it with a tabulated head-to-head on held-out data across seeds and a stated cost multiplier, and a new object that is cheaper on one experiment and 5x dearer on another is reported as a cost/benefit curve rather than a drop-in replacement - because "negligible in the grand scheme" is a claim about a budget, and budgets are where surrogates quietly stop being affordable exactly on the large models we care about.**

At 51M that is sigma2/sigma3 (peak 1.747 ± 0.120 across four seeds) and it correlates with validation loss at |r| = 0.738. At 124M the paper ranks all five candidates by their loss correlation, and sigma2/sigma3 - the boundary that WAS the edge at 51M - comes **last** at 0.211, while sigma3/sigma4 wins at 0.870. The author then writes that "the correct spectral edge automatically emerges as the ratio most strongly coupled to training dynamics", which is selection on the outcome stated as if it were a property of the object. There is no a-priori rule for which ratio is the edge at a new scale. Mechanical rule for us: **any boundary, threshold or rank we define as the argmax of a ratio over a candidate family ships with the full candidate table, the rank of the winner against the outcome it explains, and an explicit note when that ranking chose it - and the word "emerged" is reserved for cases where the winner was fixed before the outcome was measured; otherwise we write "selected", and the selected statistic has to be cross-validated on held-out windows before it counts as predictive.** Cross-reference run 714 (spread-versus-integral ranking: the naive summary ranks the random-init collapse at the top while the integral ranks the real specialists - the same trap inside the model's own features), run 712 (a percentile threshold is stable where a maximum swings two orders of magnitude).

This folder has met the same structural error from the other direction (run 706: an inflated norm will usually reproduce an effect you attributed to structure), but this is the cleanest statement of it at the level of a *null* rather than a control. - **Pattern:** **The paper's own conclusion is the opposite of what its title suggests, and it is the folder's cleanest statement of "necessary in this model, dispensable in the family" - every one of the three circuit members is individually absent from an architecture that still has sinks.** Query biases (nullified here at 44.7% of baseline) are missing entirely from many reported architectures; MLPs can be dropped from the block (50.3% here) and sinks persist in MLP-free transformers; positional encodings can be removed (17.5% here) and sinks persist in models trained without them. The authors read this as optimisation reconstructing an equivalent sink from whatever components are available, so the parameter-level pathway is an *implementation*, not *the mechanism*. Mechanical rule for us: **when we identify the pathway carrying a behaviour, we report beside it every known architecture in which the behaviour persists without that pathway, and if any exist we write "one implementation" and never "the cause" - because a necessity result in one model and a dispensability result across a family are both facts, and reporting only the first reads a property of a draw as a property of the phenomenon.** Cross-reference run 714 (a circuit necessary in s42 and absent in s271, the same structure at seed granularity), run 713 (ablation damage is architecture-dependent), run 705 (collapsing a selector reveals which half was the mechanism).

Mechanical rule for us: **every ablation or steering claim we publish names the alternative explanation it defeats and exhibits a control that differs from the treatment on that axis alone, holding size, position and machinery fixed - because a control matched on parameter count but not on the axis where the doubt lives tests nothing, and the three pairs here are the template for how to pick the axis.** Cross-reference run 706 (the norm-matched control that turned a correlation into a mechanism), run 707 (magnitude and direction separated by three ratios), run 700 (a gain needs a null that spends the same budget).
- **Pattern:** **A mitigation that moves a statistic is not a mitigation that removes the phenomenon - this paper's best intervention relocates the sink instead of deleting it, and says so.** Replacing the first positional encoding takes BOS attention from 0.563 to 0.017, which reads as a near-total fix; but the authors' own framing is that the circuit *controls sink location*, so what actually happened is that attention moved to a different position, and the residual after every pathway intervention is reported as unexplained secondary contributors rather than as zero. Mechanical rule for us: **every sink-suppression or feature-ablation result we report carries the statistic at the treated address *and* the maximum of that statistic at any other address, because a 3%-of-baseline reading is compatible both with a real fix and with a sink that relocated to position 2, and only the pair distinguishes them.** Cross-reference run 711 (gating deletes NOP sinks and multiplies broadcast sinks fortyfold), run 713 (ablation damage varies by family because each family answers "what else could carry this" differently), run 705 (removal versus relocation at the component level).

- **Pattern:** **A trajectory feature must be an integral, not a peak and not a spread - and this entry is the sharpest demonstration in the folder of why, because the artifact it defeats is one the folder has been treating as a finding.** Pythia's layer-0 heads begin at a participation ratio near 60 (random attention spreads mass across all positions, so the effective rank is high at initialisation) and collapse to 2-30 by the end of training, so ranking heads by spread - max minus min - puts exactly those collapsing heads at the top; ranking by the time integral of the clipped positive part demotes them and surfaces heads that *gain* sustained rank. The head-to-head table makes the size of the error visible: precision-at-30 is 0.93 for spread against 0.97 for the integral, but mean selectivity in the top five is 155x against 5,791x. Note what this does to every entry in this folder that read a dominant direction or a high rank out of a final checkpoint: a high effective rank is the *default* state of a random head, so the interesting quantity is not how high the rank is but how long it stayed high relative to where it started. Mechanical rule for us: **every trajectory-derived feature we define is specified as a functional of the whole curve - monotone in sustained behaviour, clipped or baseline-subtracted against its value at initialisation, and normalised by fraction of training rather than raw step count - and we print the spread-based and peak-based alternatives beside it, because on this panel the naive alternatives rank the random-init collapse as the top result while the integral ranks the actual specialists.** Cross-reference run 712 (a percentile threshold is stable while the maximum swings two orders of magnitude - the same lesson, one statistic upstream), run 708 (a scale at initialisation decides what the fit finds later).
- **Pattern:** **A circuit can be causally necessary in one seed and causally irrelevant in another trained on identical data with identical hyperparameters - the six-seed cross-ablation matrix is the cleanest negative in the folder and it constrains every "the circuit for X" claim we will ever make.** s42 implements the retrieval task with four layer-0 heads; s271 uses L6H{1,10} plus L7H{9,15} with no layer-0 head above a spread of 11. Ablating s271's circuit on s42 changes probe accuracy by nothing at any checkpoint (0.982 / 0.838 / 0.995 against baselines 0.982 / 0.843 / 0.995), and removing all 32 heads in L6+L7 from s42 still leaves 0.94 - so s271's implementation is not merely redundant on s42, it is absent. The reverse direction is not symmetric (s42's heads do hurt s271), and the seed with the broader late-layer circuit generalises better out of distribution. Note the mechanism the author draws from it: s42's circuit is an *instance* and s271's is a *class*. Mechanical rule for us: **no circuit or feature set is reported as "the" implementation of a capability without a same-architecture, different-seed ablation matrix, and where only one run exists we write "one implementation observed" rather than the definite article - because a causal necessity result on a single seed is a statement about one draw from a distribution over implementations, and this panel measured that distribution and found it spans layer 0 to layer 7.** Cross-reference run 712 (the formation circuit and the final circuit share only a third of their heads), run 704 (the head that fires on apostrophes and is otherwise silent).
- **Pattern:** **Screening quality and causal adequacy are different axes, and the gap between them is filled by distribution rather than dilution - the 43% / 77% / 100% ladder on one model is the measurement.** On Pythia 410M, top-6 spectral picks drop induction by 43%, a mech-interp-plus-second-class set by 77%, and the all-head screen at 50x by 100% with eleven heads, only three of which were in the spectral top-30. The unattractive explanation (dilution: we captured less of the circuit) and the attractive one (distribution: the circuit is spread over more heads at lower per-head selectivity) are separated by the fact that the full set of induction-selective heads exists and restores the whole effect. Mechanical rule for us: **when a screened set recovers only part of a causal effect we do not report the shortfall as noise or as a smaller mechanism - we run the exhaustive screen at a permissive threshold and check whether the missing effect is spread across heads the ranked screen did not surface, because a pre-filter's recall is bounded by the ranking it uses and the residual effect is exactly where that bound bites; and any circuit-size claim we publish carries its ablation-floor curve across thresholds, not a single point.** Cross-reference run 696 (a per-unit worth is a property of the ablated set), run 712 (a head that stopped showing the screened pattern was still inside the circuit).

- **Pattern:** **The survey's one structural claim worth carrying is that its eleven accounts are arranged by the *kind* of thing each explains, not by which is right - and that arrangement is the audit this folder has been missing.** The five levels are mathematical origin (softmax no-op; structural bias from causal masking and RoPE), training dynamics (active-dormant head reinforcement - the only account placed on that level), numerical mechanism (outlier circuits; outlier-driven rescaling; mix-compress-refine), geometric structure (geometric anchoring; anti-overmixing; spectral-energy association), and functional role (implicit attention bias). Placed against entries 704-712, this folder holds an independent reading of nearly every one of them, which converts the survey from a source of new mechanism into a **coverage and redundancy check**: the levels with only one account each in the whole literature are training dynamics and functional role, and those are exactly the levels where our own predictive ambitions sit. Mechanical rule for us: **whenever we add an account of a mechanism, we record which level it operates on and which other accounts occupy that level, and an account that is the sole occupant of its level is treated as untested rather than as established - because "no competitor" in this literature means "no one has built one", not "it survived".** Cross-reference run 704 (path-product bound: a mathematical-origin-level account), run 706 (link-by-link weight trace: numerical-mechanism level), run 710/711 (training-dynamics level, where every entry had to import its own dynamics experiment).
- **Pattern:** **Survey evidence is second-hand, and this document shows how second-hand it is at the level of the single number that the whole no-op account rests on.** The two classified evidence it marshals for the no-op family are observational (sink tokens have small value states, across BERT, ViT, LLaMA, OLMo and KV-quantization work) and causal (relax the sum-to-one constraint and the sink goes away - gating, clipped softmax, a `+1` denominator, an unnormalized rectified softmax, plain sigmoid), and every magnitude it quotes is inherited from the cited paper rather than re-measured; the survey's own study count is given as "over 210", "over 200" and "over 180" in three different sections. Note what this does to the *causal* half specifically: it is exactly the move runs 705-711 showed can be a relocation rather than a removal. Mechanical rule for us: **no survey-sourced number enters our own writing as a measurement - it enters as a pointer to the primary paper, and any account we adopt on survey authority alone is marked unverified until we have read the cited primary source; and where a survey's own internal counts disagree, that disagreement is recorded rather than averaged.** Cross-reference run 708 (a stability claim worth more as a curve than as a point), run 711 (mitigation success scored as a relocation), run 706 (the norm-matched control that made a correlation into a mechanism).
- **Pattern:** **Whether a sink "matters" is an architecture-level fact, not a sink-level one - and the survey's ablation table is the folder's widest cross-architecture sample of that.** ViTs degrade severely when their sink tokens are ablated; diffusion transformers lose almost nothing in text alignment but shift fine-grained perceptual structure by roughly six times a random-masking control; diffusion language models barely degrade at all because their sinks move during generation instead of sitting at a fixed position; MoE LLMs collapse entirely when three of several thousand experts are pruned; and in DiTs the sink carries semantic scene information rather than nullity, so the null-token reading of the word does not survive contact with that family. Read together with runs 704-712 this means the folder's most portable finding is a *conditional*: a sink is load-bearing to the degree the model's computation has been routed through the address. Mechanical rule for us: **every claim that a component is causally necessary is reported with the architecture family it was measured in and the ablation's damage on the sub-task the mechanism is supposed to serve, and a single-family ablation is never generalized into a statement about sinks as such - because the same ablation that zeroes a benchmark in one family leaves another family's quality unchanged, and the difference is the architecture's answer to "what else could carry this".** Cross-reference run 704 (deleting the first token zeroes RULER at 4096 context in Gemma 7B while costing nothing in a model trained without a fixed beginning token), run 711 (gating deletes NOP sinks and multiplies broadcast sinks fortyfold - the same family-internal version of the same lesson).
